papers.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
papers.abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

papers.title: SpecSearch: Towards Hardware-Aware Efficient Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.

papers.title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
papers.abstract: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.

papers.title: CodeReel: Accelerating Code-to-Video Agents with Exact Frame Reuse and Blocking-Aware Scheduling
papers.abstract: Coding agents make videos by writing and refining programs in a build--inspect--edit loop. A finished film costs a median of $2.85 in model calls and 11 minutes, over a third of that time in builds that block the agent. We find that much of this time is avoidable, for two reasons. First, 37.5% of the frames of a session's later films were drawn before, many shifted in time or inside an edited scene. Second, half of the builds stop at a check, where the agent needs only the verdict, but which builds stop is unknown until the checks finish. We present CodeReel, a training-free execution layer behind agents' existing commands. Exact frame reuse keys each frame by its drawing commands, regardless of its position in time, and reuses each frame whose key recurs. Blocking-aware scheduling runs the checks first and starts the render alongside them, at idle priority, unless the session's recent builds make a pass unlikely. Scheduling spends CPU to answer sooner and reuse returns it; exact keys let later versions use frames rendered for a failed one as the agent thinks. We introduce EditLoop, a benchmark of replayable agent sessions whose films are checked against renders from scratch. On it, CodeReel cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against Rebuild, a warm pipeline with parallel rendering, and by 57.9% against Sequential, today's step-by-step pipeline. On time-shifting edits its reuse renders 43.9%, close to the 43.0% whose pixels are new, while Manim-style caching renders 99.8%. With real agents, the median wait per build is 0.62x Rebuild's in Claude Code, on topics never used in development, and 0.67x in Codex CLI. The gain holds for five models and two frameworks.

papers.title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
papers.abstract: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.

papers.title: Angelfish: Leader, DAG, or Anywhere in Between
papers.abstract: To maximize performance, many modern blockchain systems rely on eventually synchronous, Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus protocols. Two protocol designs have emerged in this space: protocols that minimize latency using a leader that drives both data dissemination and consensus, and protocols that maximize throughput using a separate, asynchronous data dissemination layer. Recent protocols such as Partially Synchronous Bullshark and Sailfish combine elements of both approaches by using a DAG to enable parallel data dissemination and a leader that paces DAG formation. This improves latency while achieving state-of-the-art throughput. Yet leader-based protocols still achieve better latency under moderate loads, which are common in practice. We present Angelfish, a hybrid protocol that adapts smoothly across this design space, from leader-based to Sailfish-like DAG-based consensus. Angelfish lets a dynamically adjusted subset of parties use best-effort broadcast to issue lightweight votes instead of reliably broadcasting costlier DAG vertices. This reduces communication, helps lagging nodes catch up, and lowers latency in practice compared to prior DAG-based protocols. Our empirical evaluation shows that Angelfish attains state-of-the-art peak throughput while significantly lowering latency under moderate load, delivering the best of both worlds.

papers.title: Collecting Infrastructure-Level Measures for Energy Analysis in Modern Computing Infrastructures
papers.abstract: Modern HPC facilities are complex environments in which all components are tightly coupled; consequently, precisely modeling and accounting for energy consumption requires approaches that go beyond instrumenting individual compute nodes. Aiming for a cluster-wide vision, we designed a scalable data collection pipeline that aggregates fine-grained measurements from multiple subsystems-spanning component loads, software and hardware counters, sensors and energy-ensuring consistent sampling frequencies and synchronized data acquisition across the infrastructure. We present a dataset of comprehensive metrics collected at 1 Hz over one month from a production research data center supporting heterogeneous workloads, including HPC, Kubernetes services, and distributed storage. To illustrate what this approach makes possible in practice, we analyze two case studies-distributed I/O and large-language-model inference-showing how cluster-wide measurement reveals system-level dynamics missed by localized instrumentation. The proposed dataset and collection methodology provide a foundation for future work on predictive modeling, energy-aware resource management, and more efficient computing infrastructures.

papers.title: TAILROLL: Tail-Aware Rollout Acceleration for RL-Based LLM Post-Training
papers.abstract: RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) is bottlenecked by rollout: heavy-tailed responses leave engines idle as each step waits for the longest response. Asynchronous training masks, but does not eliminate, idle time. We distinguish imbalance waste (uneven placement and decode contention) from straggler waste (waiting for the longest response). Tail length, not average load, often sets the step bound. We propose TAILROLL, an online scheduler integrated into an open-source RL framework. It combines stateless in-flight migration and sufficiency-gated termination. Migration moves decoding requests between engines at chunk boundaries and resumes them with one re-prefill under a freeness-based, cost-aware tail-balancing policy. Termination stops a response when its GRPO group has enough completed samples for advantage estimation, masking its partial output from the training loss. Across ten configurations, TAILROLL reduces rollout bubble ratio by 21% to 74% and cross-engine KV-cache imbalance by 44% to 79%. In end-to-end RL training, it cuts rollout time by 24% to 34%, full step time by 21% to 22% on long-CoT RL, and p95 request latency by 28% to 37%, while raising generation throughput by up to 33% with comparable or higher final reward.

papers.title: XM-Sparse: High-Throughput Sparse-Attention LLM Serving over Scale-up Memory Pools
papers.abstract: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.

papers.title: CheckCo: Checkpoint-Coordinated Load Balancingfor Skewed Event Streams at Scale
papers.abstract: Event streams are rarely uniform: a few dominant keys can generate orders of magnitude more events than the rest, overloading the workers that receive them and capping throughput. We present CheckCo, a checkpoint-coordinated load-balancing algorithm built on a dynamic oracle that estimates per-key frequencies from the live stream, with no prior statistics. Workers count events per key locally; at each checkpoint barrier, the counts are merged into a partitioning function that divides each key into a number of splits roughly proportional to its estimated frequency and packs the splits onto workers, and this function routes the next checkpoint window. We derive approximation bounds on the resulting load imbalance from classical scheduling results and bound its total key fan-out. On a production pipeline processing over 100 billion events per day, the most loaded worker receives only 9.8% more events than the average over a day (imbalance ratio 1.10), against 8.03 for key-based routing in simulation; in simulation, CheckCo also needs less than half the fan-out of earlier partitioners that reach comparable balance. Shifts in the key distribution are reflected in routing from the next checkpoint on, and the load stays balanced through job restarts.

papers.title: Byzantine Resilience of Robot Gathering under Round-Robin Scheduling
papers.abstract: We study deterministic gathering of $n$ anonymous, oblivious mobile robots in the plane under round-robin scheduling with rigid movement, in the presence of $f$ Byzantine robots. Robots observe all robot positions with their multiplicities, while their local coordinate systems may change adversarially between activations. The goal is for all correct robots to gather at a single point in finite time and remain there forever. We analyze ToMax, a simple algorithm that moves to a point of maximum multiplicity and stays still if and only if its current position is the unique maximum. We prove that ToMax achieves gathering whenever $f\le\lfloor\sqrt{n}/2\rfloor$, establishing an $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ lower bound on the achievable Byzantine resilience.

papers.title: Similarity-Aware Client-Side Reordering for Server-Side Storage Compression in Distributed File Systems
papers.abstract: As growing data volumes strain the capacity of distributed file systems, server-side storage compression transparently reduces disk usage, but its effectiveness is limited when similar blocks land in separate compression records and cannot share matches. We present a client-side reordering framework that transforms the physical block layout before persistence, so that related blocks are co-located within the same compression scope without replacing the existing storage-server compressor. It operates on bounded reordering windows, periodically selects among candidate layouts via lightweight compression of sampled data, and recovers the original logical order during reads with compact window-local metadata. We implement the framework in the SkyFS distributed file system, using the Zstandard (Zstd) compressor on the OpenZFS storage backend. Results on diverse datasets show that the framework reduces physical storage by up to 42.9% relative to logical-order writes, while achieving 94-108% of baseline sequential-read throughput and 91-99% of random-read IOPS. Client-side layout construction is the primary additional write cost, showing that adaptive similarity-aware reordering substantially improves storage efficiency with acceptable overhead.

papers.title: SPICE: Sparse Parameter Gossip for LLM Pretraining
papers.abstract: Pretraining language models across geographically distributed resources requires communication-efficient methods that operate under limited and variable internet bandwidth. Decentralized training replaces global collectives with peer exchanges, but full-model messages make larger peer neighborhoods costly. We introduce SPICE, which combines sparse parameter gossip with error feedback through corrected parameter values that remain directly interpretable as peer neighborhoods change. These sparse exchanges make broader neighborhoods affordable, achieving better training quality with less communication than the evaluated dense decentralized baselines. As the replica count grows, SPICEincreases the number of peers contacted while keeping individual messages sparse, limiting the quality degradation observed with dense gossip. Under bandwidth constraints, SPICE achieves higher training throughput than DDP and dense gossip, while sustaining throughput during transient link slowdowns.

papers.title: Flux: Optimal Scheduling of Optical Circuit Switches for LLM Training
papers.abstract: Optical Circuit Switching (OCS) offers high bandwidth density and energy efficiency for LLM training, but incurs a non-negligible reconfiguration delay. Prior work typically schedules optical circuit switches independently of compute, using aggregate traffic demand to determine which circuits to provision and when. We argue that this separation creates a fundamental inefficiency: reconfigurations that ignore the compute timeline can stall communication, resulting in low circuit utilization and large buffer requirements. In this paper, we present Flux, a scheduler that optimally schedules optical circuit switches based on the structure of the entire workload. Flux remains effective across a wide range of switching speeds by reusing circuits and amortizing reconfiguration delay behind compute and communication. We show that Flux reduces training iteration time by up to $10\times$ and peak NIC buffer requirements by more than three orders of magnitude compared to traditional periodic schedulers.

papers.title: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling
papers.abstract: GPU acceleration of finite element assembly is well established for standard formulations, but mixed-dimensional problems, in which volumetric subdomains are coupled via lower-dimensional interfaces, remain unsupported in automated frameworks such as FEniCS. We extend cuDOLFINx, a GPU-enabled extension of the DOLFINx finite element framework, to assemble such interface problems on GPUs while preserving the high-level FEniCS programming model. Combined with GPU-resident Krylov solvers and algebraic multigrid preconditioning, this enables end-to-end GPU execution of the EMI (Extracellular--Membrane--Intracellular) model, an elliptic interface problem from cardiac modeling in which many intracellular subdomains are coupled through membranes. We compare the GPU implementation against a CPU-based one through strong and weak scaling experiments on regular and realistic 3D cardiac geometries with up to 8000 cells and 22 million degrees of freedom. In terms of assembly, a single GH200 node is roughly equivalent to two 144-core CPU nodes in strong scaling, and to two to three nodes in weak scaling, depending on geometry. For the linear solver, performance depends on geometry, preconditioning, and problem scale. On the regular geometry, GPU advantages emerge mainly at larger problem sizes and node counts. On the realistic geometry, with the same algebraic multigrid preconditioner for both architectures, the GPU is faster at all tested scales. The implementation is available as open-source software and applies to other problems with interface coupling.

papers.title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
papers.abstract: AI's inflection point is a fountain of risks for digital platforms, as those in control of global platforms cede control of the algorithms, membership and content to AI: (i) AI control of global platforms used by the majority of humanity; (ii) unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals; and (iii) unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, which people cannot distinguish from genuine content. Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon: a social contract that can be freely adopted by any group of people, where groups bound by the same contract can union by mutual consent, possibly into a single global union. Grassroots contracts are realised by grassroots platforms, person-to-person platforms owned, operated and governed by their participants. We developed, with AI, a methodology to compile grassroots contracts to working smartphone apps. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two, and show how they corral these risks: (i) grassroots platforms are not controlled by a third party who may cede control to AI; (ii) AI agents are introduced with accountability: similarly to cars, their manufacturers are accountable for manufacturing defects and their operators for reckless operation; and (iii) every item carries the signatures of its author and of every agent that forwarded it, so creators and forwarders of harmful content are accountable and culpable. Much work remains for grassroots apps to be competitive with incumbent global platforms; but perhaps now this could be achieved with some AI-months rather than with incalculably-many person-years.

papers.title: JigSLO: Solving the Resource Puzzle for Efficient Multi-LLM Serving
papers.abstract: GPU spatial sharing co-locates instances with complementary demands, such as compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode, promising cost-efficient multi-LLM serving. Prior systems partition compute and coordinate shared memory capacity, but do not model bandwidth contention among co-located instances of heterogeneous LLMs. This contention makes each instance's latency depend on the memory-access patterns of its co-runners, even when its own resource allocation remains unchanged. Drawing on extensive measurements, we find that the latency impact of bandwidth contention can be captured by a time-shared memory-access model with contended and uncontended periods, so the overall latency can be analytically estimated as a time-weighted average of the latency estimates for these periods. We propose JigSLO, a contention-aware multi-LLM serving system that manages memory resources and schedules each model's prefill and decode phases as separate instances, treating their co-location as a placement decision. Its contention-aware predictor estimates per-instance latency under any co-location from standalone profiles alone. Guided by these predictions, its placement algorithm jointly selects each instance's tensor parallelism, compute share, and batch configuration, pairing complementary memory-access patterns to maximize throughput within each model's latency targets. JigSLO's shared resource manager complements this on the capacity side, sharing weights, pooling KV cache, and transferring it between prefill and decode instances. Across three datasets covering chat, code generation, and long-context summarization, JigSLO outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by $2.3\times$ in SLO attainment and $1.2\times$ in throughput on average, matching their best attainment with half the GPUs on long-context workloads.

papers.title: AInfer-PD: Communication-Safe In-Place Prefill-Decode Multiplexing for Distributed MoE Rollouts
papers.abstract: In agentic reinforcement learning (RL), asynchronous multi-turn trajectories repeatedly introduce continuation prefills (P) while other trajectories remain in decode (D). Efficient rollout completion therefore requires D to advance during long P executions. In-place multiplexing shares devices, model weights, and KV state, but phase-specific communication in distributed MoE introduces two constraints: cross-rank collective ordering and ownership of mutable communication state. Whole-prefill coordination can ensure safe ordering but delays D. DeepEP's normal and low-latency paths suit large P and small D batches, respectively, but safely overlapping them requires separating their mutable communication state. We present AInfer-PD, which extends in-place P/D multiplexing to distributed MoE rollouts. AInfer-PD establishes rank-consistent collective ordering at safe communication boundaries, allowing successive D iterations to advance without waiting for an entire prefill execution to be enqueued or completed. It gives P and D separate communication buffers and protocol state within one DeepEP runtime, allowing P to use the normal path while D retains the low-latency path. Together, these mechanisms preserve useful P/D overlap while sharing model weights and KV storage on the same devices. Across repeated single-node prefill-intensive workloads, AInfer-PD reduces fixed-workload rollout completion time by 7.1-22.5% relative to the same AInfer engine with P/D multiplexing disabled and by 24.8-32.9% relative to SGLang. On two nodes, the reductions are 18.0-35.3% and 18.3-31.8%, respectively. In a same-engine ablation, fine-grained boundaries reduce completion time by a further 8.6-19.8% over whole-prefill asynchronous enqueue.

papers.title: Why Kubernetes Cannot Contain a Full Lazy-Pulling Cache: Two Impossibility Results and a Bounded, Honest Design for Model Serving
papers.abstract: Lazy container-image pulling makes cold starts of autoscaled model-serving fleets on Kubernetes nearly independent of model size, but it moves the model's bytes into a node-level cache that the platform neither bounds nor accounts for. This article establishes, by experiment, two impossibility results for that cache. A monitoring-side remedy cannot catch its failure: a sentinel readiness probe stays green while 272 of 280 files are unreadable. A platform-side remedy cannot contain it: kubelet, given full disk-pressure visibility, frees 0 bytes by image garbage collection and falls back to evicting pods (26 across the campaign, the reading pod among them), because its reclamation actuator is keyed to an accounting that does not know the cache exists. The article then eliminates the failure class inside the component that owns the bytes, with no change to kubelet or the container runtime interface, by two design rules: a byte budget whose pressure signal is keyed to filesystem truth, so that a never-blocking, lossy accounting still enforces a hard bound (held against about 301,000 dropped updates), and pass-through semantics under which a failed cache write never becomes a failed read, with the coupling traced to a single io.MultiWriter. Across six pre-specified campaigns on AWS, upstream stargz-snapshotter fails 273 of 280 model files at 90% cache pre-fill; the proposed system reads all 150.3 GB with zero errors at +18.5% completion cost and holds the budget under a live read, co-tenancy, and a three-node fleet. A source audit shows the missing bound generalizes to SOCI and Nydus. The implementation is open source and has been proposed upstream.

papers.title: IA-MoE: An Intensity-Aware Mixture of Experts for DNN Inference
papers.abstract: In edge-cloud collaborative inference, the layers of a deep neural network (DNN) are placed on edge and cloud virtual machines (VMs) for every request, while the edge load and the cross-cloud bandwidth change over time. We propose IA-MoE, an intensity-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework that scores each layer-VM pair by end-to-end delay and energy and places the layers one at a time on the best-scoring VM. Such greedy placement is myopic when trained on per-layer labels: offloading to the cloud slows the first offloaded layer while the gain appears only in later layers, so the policy keeps too many requests at the edge. Training on the remaining request time after each decision removes this myopia and reduces the mean delay by 12-56% on congested workloads. In CloudSimSDN simulations with three DNNs and two public request traces, IA-MoE has the lowest mean delay of all compared methods on congested VGG16 workloads, across cross-cloud bandwidths of 150-600 Mbps, fluctuating bandwidth and saturated edge servers. A random forest trained on the same label is 5-27% slower, and only a heuristic that sends whole requests to the cloud uses less energy, at up to 20 times the delay. When the edge is lightly loaded, offloading does not pay and simple heuristics perform as well. IA-MoE also beats a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent with the same features in all 19 tested settings, with a mean delay lower by a factor of 1.3 to 10.5, and trains in minutes instead of hours.
